title: Barry Nalebuff | Split The Pie: A Radical New Way to Negotiate | Talks at Google
description:
Barry Nalebuff discusses his latest book "Split The Pie: A Radical New Way to Negotiate", a radical, principled, and field-tested approach that identifies what’s really at stake in any negotiation and ensures you get your half—so you can focus on growing the pie. 

Negotiation is stressful. It can bring out the worst in people. Wouldn’t it be better if there were a principled way to negotiate? Wouldn’t it be even better if there were a way to treat people fairly and get treated fairly in a negotiation? Barry Nalebuff does just that in "Split the Pie" via a simple, practical method that reveals the true power of the players and what they bring to the table. He offers a theory-based and field-tested approach to negotiation illustrated with examples and in-depth case studies. You’ll see how it helped reframe a high-stakes negotiation when Coca-Cola purchased Honest Tea, a company Barry co-founded with his former student Seth Goldman. The pie framework also works for everyday negotiations. You’ll learn how to deploy pie logic to determine truly equitable solutions, and employ empathy to expand the pie and sell your solution. "Split the Pie" allows both sides to focus their energy on making the biggest possible pie.

Barry Nalebuff is the Milton Steinbach Professor at Yale School of Management where he has taught for over thirty years. An expert on game theory, he has written extensively on its application to business strategy, including his best sellers Thinking Strategically, The Art of Strategy, and Mission in a Bottle. He advised the NBA in their prior negotiations with the Players Association, as well as several firms in major merger and acquisition transactions. He is also a serial entrepreneur: his ventures include Honest Tea, Kombrewcha, and Choose Health. A graduate of MIT, a Rhodes Scholar and a Junior Fellow at the Harvard Society of Fellows, Barry earned his doctorate at Oxford University.

Get the book here: https://goo.gle/36zhJuf.

Moderated by Hal Varian.
summary: Barry Nalebuff argues that in negotiations, the goal is not to divide the total value available but to identify and divide only the incremental value created by reaching an agreement. He illustrates this by explaining that when a domain name is taken in bad faith, the negotiation is not over who owns the domain, but rather over the cost of the dispute resolution process required to secure it.

transcript: [MUSIC PLAYING] HAL VARIAN: Hi. I'm Hal Varian. I'm the chief economist here at Google. And it's my great pleasure to introduce Barry Nalebuff. I have known Barry since 1980, when we met at Oxford. He was a student. I was an assistant professor visiting Oxford for a year. And we had many exciting intellectual conversations about economics. And we've remained friends ever since. So Barry is the Milton Steinbach Professor at Yale School of Management. He teaches negotiation, innovation, strategy, and game theory. And he's written two fantastic books-- one, "Thinking Strategically," and the other, "The Art of Strategy." Both of them are great books. I had a little involvement in the first one. I twisted his arm a little bit and said, this is great stuff, you should write a book. And by gosh, he went out and did it. He's been a very successful entrepreneur as well, co-founding the Honest Tea company. And he wrote a book about that experience as well called "Mission in a Bottle." And that's one of the very, very few comic books, illustrated novels that's written by a professor at Yale as far as I know. He's got a new book coming out soon called "Split The Pie." And that's about the art and science of negotiation. And he's been kind enough to come visit us-- at least virtually-- and tell us about the book. So Barry, I understand that in this book there's an interaction with a troll-- or so it was said. BARRY NALEBUFF: Sure. Well, first, let me just start with a little bit more background in my introduction with Hal. Hal was my first co-author. Back in 1981, we wrote a paper together about risk sharing in non-classical environments that probably neither of us really remember. But it was-- HAL VARIAN: [LAUGHS] BARRY NALEBUFF: --a paper about what to do in risk sharing when there are economies of scale-- something like a patent race, where you only care about who comes in first. And I got a free trip to Sweden as part of that. So I-- thank you for my introduction. Not only was he my first co-author-- in some ways, he was my first teacher. Because when I grew up as an economist, everybody used his textbook. It was the way that we all started learning economics. And yes, he was the one who introduced me to my publisher at WW Norton. I think he got a small stake of what ended up being a book, which has now sold 500,000 copies. So that was a great win-win that we had there. And also, invited me to be part of Google working on a potential partnership you had with your friends at-- oh, my god. Are they even still existing anymore? HAL VARIAN: Split Video? BARRY NALEBUFF: Yahoo. HAL VARIAN: Yahoo. BARRY NALEBUFF: Yahoo, exactly. Working as a way of bringing Google's ad technology to Yahoo. And somehow, the DOJ didn't really quite understand what was going on there. So thank you. It's an honor to be here with you. And let me explain what I'm talking about in terms of "Split The Pie" and then bring that into the case of the negotiation with an online troll. What's funny about negotiation is that the way economists see what's going on is completely different from the way that the rest of the world does. And as a result, people misunderstand what they're negotiating about. So here's a simple example to illustrate that. Alice and Bob are negotiating over a twelve-slice pizza. They have to agree on how to divide it up. Otherwise, they don't get it. But if they don't reach an agreement, Alice will get four slices, and Bob will get two. The way the world sees that negotiation is that Alice is twice as strong as Bob. So Alice should get twice as much as Bob. Therefore, divide the pizza eight and four. Other people think, no, the fair outcome is you take the 12 slices, you divide them six and six. But the way I learned about things in economics from Hal is to think about incremental value that's created-- and that if they don't reach an agreement, Alice and Bob will get four plus two slices, or six in total. If they do reach an agreement, they'll get 12. So the purpose of the agreement, the purpose of the negotiation is to go from six to 12. Those incremental six slices are what the negotiation is about. Alice needs Bob every bit as much as Bob needs Alice. Therefore, they have equal power. Power and fairness say they should divide those six slices three and three. So what Alice gets is the four from no agreement plus three-- or 7. And what Bob gets is the two from no agreement plus three-- and 5. Right? That's how an economist would see it. And what's crazy is the rest of the world does not appreciate this. And therefore, they get all confused about what the negotiation is. They make arguments about the 12 slices and not about how to divide the six. OK. So here's an example of how this happened-- this pie approach was useful in a real-life negotiation. I have this friend who's an idiot. This friend decided to file for a trademark on his own without hiring a lawyer to save some money. And what he didn't realize is that trademark applications are public when you make them. Because of course, other people have to be able to respond to the trademark. They have to be able to object to it. You can't keep it hidden. Well, when it became public, this troll, who I'll call Edward-- because that's his name-- HAL VARIAN: [LAUGHS] BARRY NALEBUFF: --went and bought the URL .com-- the URL associated with the trademark. And my friend goes to register it, discovers it has just been taken that day, and writes to Edward, who says, oh, yeah, I'm happy to sell it to you for $2,500. And sometimes in negotiation, we'd call this an anchoring effect. He's out there trying to really soften up the other side. So what should my friend do? Well, he's an idiot, but he's not stupid. And so he does a little googling and discovers that there's an organization called ICANN, the domain registry that resolves disputes. And what Edward has done is called registration in bad faith. And essentially, if you go to ICANN, ICANN will restore the domain name to my friend. The cost of the ICANN dispute process is $1,300. And it's virtually guaranteed to be successful. In fact, if you do a little bit more googling, you discover that Edward has lost every time he's gone up to ICANN. He has a history of doing this. So my friend writes back and says, look, forget the $2,500. I'd rather go to ICANN and pay them $1,300 and you get $0. And so Edward writes back and says, OK, $1,100. And now is time to discuss what the pie is. So my friend values the domain name at $10,000, at $20,000-- really wants this domain name. So Hal, what do you think the pie is in this case here? HAL VARIAN: Ah. [LAUGHS] Put me on the spot, huh? BARRY NALEBUFF: Yeah. Well, it's-- reverse the roles here a little bit. So what is the negotiation about? HAL VARIAN: So the question is, if he gets the domain, what does he do with it? That is-- BARRY NALEBUFF: Oh, he's going to be starting a new company, in fact. HAL VARIAN: Well, I mean the other guy. BARRY NALEBUFF: Oh, Edward has zero use for this domain name. HAL VARIAN: Exactly. That was my point. So zero use from his point of view. BARRY NALEBUFF: Correct. HAL VARIAN: They've got one where it's a huge value. BARRY NALEBUFF: Huge value. HAL VARIAN: Thousands of dollars. And you've got the other that gets zero out of it. BARRY NALEBUFF: Yeah. HAL VARIAN: So-- well, I'm not sure I know-- I haven't read your book, so I'm not sure I know the answer to the question. But I will say I'd consider calling his bluff, saying, no, too much. There's other domains. I'll get them. BARRY NALEBUFF: Well, let's think about this for a moment. Whether my friend reaches a deal with Edward or doesn't, he's ending up with the domain name. Because either he's going to get it from ICANN or he's going to get it from Edward. So actually, the negotiation is not over who's going to get the domain name. It's only really over whether or not my friend is going to pay $1,300 to ICANN. And then what the two of them can do is save the $1,300. HAL VARIAN: Right, right. BARRY NALEBUFF: So it does actually matter how much the domain is worth because my friend's got that. Can they save the ICANN $1,300? And who has more power in that, Edward or my friend? Well, if Edward says, no, it's gone. And if my friend says no to the deal, it's gone. Therefore, they have, in my view, equal power. And what Edward has proposed is a split of $1,100-$200. By charging my friend $1,100, Edward would end up $1,100 ahead, and my friend would end up $200 ahead. OK. So one option is my friend could play the mirror game-- what we'll call fight fire with fire-- come back and say, look, hey, you offered me a $200 gain. I'll give you $200 for it. So there. But I think that just aggravates the other side. It escalates. You want to fight fire with water, not with fire. You want to put out the fire. So at this point, my friend explains what the negotiation is about and says, look, there's $1,300 to divide up. What you proposed is you end up $1,100 ahead, I end up $200 ahead. I don't think so. Let's split it $650-$650. And Edward comes back and says, look how far I've come down. I've come down from $2,500 to $1,100. I'll meet you halfway at $900. That's as far as I go. That's the lowest I'll go. Seal the deal. Let's make this happen. Well, first off, has Edward really come down that far? I don't think anything from $2,500 down to $1,300 should even count. Because until you're below the $1,300, there is no pie to discuss. And if you say how much he's come down, it's really from $1,100 to $900, which is $400. Whereas, my friend has gone up from $0 to $650. So my friend-- basically, what does he do? Actually, he does nothing. He doesn't even write back. Because at this point, what does Edward stand to lose? Edward stands to lose $900. My friend-- only $400. Edward is actually in a much riskier position, if you like, because he's trying to be too greedy. And a week later, Edward writes back and says, OK, let's close this deal-- $650. So what does-- oh, by the way, you've probably guessed that friend was me. HAL VARIAN: [CHUCKLES] You're your best friend? BARRY NALEBUFF: I'm my best friend. And of course, there's another moral here, which is, buy the damn domain name before you file for the trademark. That only costs you $1,250. But look, does Edward care about the pie, or does Edward care about fairness? Absolutely not. He's a troll. HAL VARIAN: Right. BARRY NALEBUFF: However, he understood that I did. And I have a principle. He has arbitrary. And principle beats arbitrary. Well, what if-- HAL VARIAN: But-- BARRY NALEBUFF: Go ahead. HAL VARIAN: But he does these dozens of times or hundreds of times. You've only done it once. This is the first time you've asked for a domain name. BARRY NALEBUFF: That's true. HAL VARIAN: So the question is-- it's true that you have the motivation, that you care about it. He doesn't. But on the other hand, he's had experience, and you haven't. But you're so smart that you don't need experience. You could figure out the logic yourself. BARRY NALEBUFF: When you have a principle, it helps-- it beats arbitrary. And people have often said in negotiations, start with a high number to soften them up. I think this-- it's called anchoring. But I think in the case of negotiation you can get sunk by your own anchor. Because if you anchor at an extreme point, you then have to make lots of big movements. And the fact that he's moved from $2,500 to $1,100 to $900 tells me he has no principle. Whereas, I don't have to move. I've given a logic to what's going on here. And if you'd like-- and I think this should appeal to the Googlers, you know-- if you like, this is the-- not Dr. Spock, who's the pediatrician, but Mr. Spock approach to negotiation. We're putting in some logic behind what's going on. And once you figure out the pie, you can explain it to the other side. And they're likely to get what's going on. HAL VARIAN: We are a registrar, by the way. BARRY NALEBUFF: You are a register? So I should have started with you right from the beginning. HAL VARIAN: [LAUGHS] Yeah. BARRY NALEBUFF: That's a great point. HAL VARIAN: OK. But let me ask you to pursue that-- another point. I was on a committee many years ago about whether we should expand the number of top-level domains. There are only the few domains that were up there. BARRY NALEBUFF: Like .com, .biz, dot-something. HAL VARIAN: And then there were country domains. And there were a couple of special cases. But we said, no-- or the people who were proposing this said, no, no, we should have dozens, if not hundreds, of more domains. So what would happen to your argument if you had that capability of an alternative name that isn't so bad-- one that's not my favorite, but it's not so bad? BARRY NALEBUFF: Actually, one of the things I wrote to him is I said that-- the domain was makeroates.com. And then I sold the company to Pepsi. So I really did want that name. I sold it to Quaker. "Quaker," "Maker--" kind of was a good play there. HAL VARIAN: Ah, OK. BARRY NALEBUFF: I did register maker-oates.com as a potential backup. But I didn't want complication. I didn't want somebody else who could possibly get confusion. And so I don't know if it was worth $5,000 or $10,000 to solve that problem. But it was certainly worth more than $1,300. And so I was prepared to go to ICANN in this particular case to get it back. That's not always going to be the case. Something else people say in negotiation is, you should never reveal your BATNA. You should never reveal your fallback. And here, I did it. Did it put me in a weak position? So he knows that my alternative is paying $1,300, but that doesn't mean I'm going to accept $1,100. He can't push me into that for the same reason why I can't push him near his BATNA of $0. He shouldn't expect me to accept $1,100 any more than I should expect him to accept $200. And therefore, once you understand the idea of the pie and splitting it, you're both going to make a lot of money relative to your BATNA. And you can now focus on how do you make the pie bigger rather than how you're splitting it up. Now, in this case, you could say it was a zero-sum game-- so I can't make the pie bigger. But actually, not reaching an agreement is a way of screwing up the pie. And so by finding a way that worked for both of us-- because I never want to ask somebody to do something that I'm not willing to do. And so therefore, if I'm saying I want to get more than half the pie, then I'm also asking them to say-- if they then say, hey, I want to get more than half the pie, we can't actually both ask for the same thing here. And that's one of the definitions of things that are unreasonable. HAL VARIAN: And if I remember correctly, in your other book "Co-Opetition" you talked a lot about making the pie bigger. Because there, cooperation even between competitors could increase the size of the return to each of them. BARRY NALEBUFF: Exactly. And in fact, that was what led to the Googlee-Yahoo deal at the time. Google is able to get more money for each AdWords search than Yahoo was. You probably were the one who ran that test to prove it. And so over time, Google will end up taking all of those Yahoo customers away, who will discover the greater value of the Google home page. But there was a period where people were stuck there because of Yahoo Finance, News, Email. And so if you could help them get more money per eyeball for the ads, then you could share in that. And that was indeed the proposal. So the goal is to think about how to expand the pie, but you can't do that if you have to watch your back the whole time about how it's going to be divided up. And so I like to start a negotiation with actually what the ground rules are. People often jump way too quickly into talking about price. And my view is you could say it the funny way, which is, hey, do you think we should agree that each of us will act like jerks, and take a zero-sum mindset, and try and screw the other as best we can? And hopefully, the other person will say, no, no, I'd rather not do that, in which case you say, OK, good. How about we've got this crazy idea called "split the pie." And let me explain to you what it's about. And let's create this big pie and split it equally. HAL VARIAN: So one case that shows up all the time in the tech world is standard setting. BARRY NALEBUFF: Mm-hmm. HAL VARIAN: So what happens is, would both be better off-- or would all be better off if there's a uniform standard for technology in the home-- things like Am-- and just recently, just in the last month or so, the top producers in that area have settled on a standardization deal that allows everything to be interoperable. BARRY NALEBUFF: Great. HAL VARIAN: So you can have one device from Google, one device from Amazon-- they'll still talk to each other just fine. So this is a big step forward for the industry as a whole, I think. And it's a great example of what you're describing. Because there's a great deal of value there, but it took years of negotiation to get it in place. BARRY NALEBUFF: Yeah. And one of the things you're pointing out is, of course, negotiations get even trickier when I have more than two people. HAL VARIAN: Yes. BARRY NALEBUFF: Because if I have A, B, and C who are negotiating with each other, if they don't reach a deal, will it be A and B who will do a deal? A and C? B and C? Or they'll each go all separate ways. And the pie is the extra value created from a deal compared to no deal. But I don't really necessarily know what the "no deal" is when I have lots of parties. Whereas, with only two, now I do know-- it's, what can I do on my own, as opposed to, what can I do with some other potential player. HAL VARIAN: Yeah. And here, of course, the larger firms in the area are the bellwethers. They're the ones that people watch. If they're getting close, then the smaller parties will join in the deal because there's a lot potentially in it for them. Anyway, who's the intended audience for your book? BARRY NALEBUFF: All the people on this podcast-- HAL VARIAN: [LAUGHS] BARRY NALEBUFF: --would be a very good start. Look, I think the truth is all of us negotiate all the time. And so it's something that we need to be able to do in a better way. And people are afraid of it because money is at stake. Reputations are at stake. You can have bad feelings. And so how do you do it in a way that is productive and allows you to take advantage of your strengths? My students at Yale are smart. They're empathetic until they start negotiating. And then they start acting like jerks because they didn't have any better way of doing it. And they're guessing that that's what you're supposed to do. And so how can we help you take advantage of your intellect, your logic and apply that to bring the emotional level down and bring the logical level up. And understanding the negotiation pie, I think, is a way to do that. HAL VARIAN: So you've taught negotiation to the policy majors, the business school majors, the economists. What about the lawyers? BARRY NALEBUFF: Oh, I teach this to some of the leading law firms in New York, the M&A lawyers. I teach this at the Yale Law School. So yes, it is something that I think has been particularly practical. A recent example one of my students told me is that he had done a deal. And the company that was the target, after all the terms were agreed to, said, if we move the negotiation fees around-- the legal fees-- we can create a bigger tax loss. And the value of that tax loss ends up being worth $30 million. And-- or actually, it's a $30 million tax loss. After taxes, it's a $50 million tax savings, I guess. And so it's our tax loss. So we should get that as part of the deal. HAL VARIAN: Ah-ha. BARRY NALEBUFF: And this lawyer who had taken my classes, [? Ascha Depai ?] said, well, it's true that we need your tax loss, but you need our profits. Because only by putting your losses together with our profits do we in fact have a tax savings. And so let's split it seven and a half-seven and a half. And he had no counter. And so you can try and be obstinate, but you look like a jerk when you do that. And it's, again, this idea that logic beats arbitrary. And it's kind of funny because people don't-- people think one side is bringing more to the table than the other. So one of the companies I'll mention I started is Honest Tea. And think about this negotiation with Coca-Cola. We were buying bottles at $0.19 a bottle, and Coke could get those exact same bottles for $0.11. So they could save $0.08 a bottle on 100 million bottles. That's $8 million. Well, if we try and divide that $8 million up proportionately-- proportional to sales, revenue-- Coke's revenue-- $40 billion. Honest Tea's revenue at the time-- $20 million. That's 2000 to one. So Coke would get $7,996,000, and we'd get $4,000. OK. That just shows you proportionality is insane. Coke says, well, look-- so I'm saying we should do it four and four. And Coke says, I don't get it. It's our purchasing power. So you can't get those savings without us. What are you bringing to the table? And the sarcastic answer is, our inefficiencies. HAL VARIAN: [LAUGHS] BARRY NALEBUFF: The truthful answer-- that is true-- is also our customers. Without our customers who are willing to buy this delicious, lightly sweetened, organic tea in an overpriced bottle, your purchasing power doesn't add up to anything. And so you've already applied your purchasing power on your products. If you want to apply them on ours, well, you need us just like actually Yahoo needed Google to apply the technology to increase the amount of money they could make on each ad. And so it's always the case that both sides are bringing the same thing, the same negotiation pie to any deal. HAL VARIAN: Yeah, I think part of the problem with amateurs is this mental accounting issue-- that, I've got this much money in this category, this much here, this much here. And one of the points you're making is, well, it's not what you have when the bargaining starts. It's what happens when you go home. And it doesn't matter where that extra dollar came from, really. BARRY NALEBUFF: Yeah, yeah. When you're measuring how much more is created compared to what we started with-- well, the whole point of the negotiation is to beat where you started from. HAL VARIAN: Yeah, yeah. BARRY NALEBUFF: And so therefore, don't double count the strength of the fallbacks. Because just because somebody has a better fallback-- that means they're going to get more. Just like Alice had four slices rather than two in the pizza example, she's going to end up with two more slices, but that doesn't mean she gets any more of the six slices they're negotiating over. HAL VARIAN: Tell us another success story about how this applied in a-- especially if you had an involvement by the students or your colleagues at Honest Tea. BARRY NALEBUFF: Well, the first time the theory of the pie moved from the academic classroom to real life was actually in my negotiations with Coca-Cola. And we had a problem. It made sense for Coke to buy the company. But at the time, our sales were $23 million. And Coke is excellent at bringing companies from $100 million to $1 billion in sales. They're also pretty good at taking a company from $50 million down to $0. And so we were too small to really fit into their system, which I'm sure is true for Google as well in the sense of if the company is too small you can get lost. And so they agreed that they would buy us in three years. And during those three years, they would help us with purchasing those $0.11 cent bottles. They would help us with distribution, with production. But now, Hal, I'm sure you can see what the problem is. HAL VARIAN: The problem is, what if they call something off during the middle? I mean, we get this situation-- BARRY NALEBUFF: No, no. HAL VARIAN: No? Couldn't do that? BARRY NALEBUFF: Let's focus on the good news-- that we're all going to happen. The problem from their perspective is they're going to help us increase our revenue, but they don't want to pay more for all the help they're providing. HAL VARIAN: Ah, OK. BARRY NALEBUFF: Right? I means-- HAL VARIAN: What's their compensation? BARRY NALEBUFF: So what are they going to get from it? And in particular, they don't want to be penalized. No good deed goes unpunished. So what we agreed in the first hour of the negotiation was, look, why are we doing this deal? It's to increase our revenue. And it's to increase our revenue more than what we could do without your help. So we think we could get to x without you. To the extent we get above x, it's only because we were working together. Therefore, you should pay full price on sales up to x. And to the extent our sales exceed x, you should pay half price. So yes, you're going to pay more for your help because you need the vehicle in which to help. We're providing the vehicle on which your distribution, purchasing, production can make something better. And we can't do without you. So we agreed in that first hour, let's create this big pie. Let's split it. And then we had a fight over what x is-- what can we do on our own. And we had a disagreement on what is the market value for sales of x-- what is the right market multiple. But those were both data questions. And if you like, what we're doing here is turning negotiation into a data exploration exercise as opposed to into a conflict. And I'm betting the people at Google are really good at those data exploration exercises. HAL VARIAN: Yeah. So your point is you could look at other acquisitions that Coke made where the numbers kind of came out or you look at-- BARRY NALEBUFF: Well, not just Coke made-- that all the-- Coke had the data on all 27 acquisitions that had been done in the beverage industry over the last decade. HAL VARIAN: I see. So they had that number as well. And that would allow them to come up with a reasonable agreement about what the data said. BARRY NALEBUFF: And we didn't have that information. They had better information than we did. We knew about some of them. They knew about every one of them. HAL VARIAN: Yeah. Huh. Very interesting. So let's see. So could I-- no, I probably can't. I was going to say, can I ask you about your royalty negotiations with your publisher. But I think there might be some things that are off limits. BARRY NALEBUFF: No, you-- so-- HAL VARIAN: No, that's OK. BARRY NALEBUFF: So it turns out I messed up here, if you like. After Hal introduced me to Drake McFeely, who is now-- well, became the CEO, and president, chairman of WW Norton. But in those days, he was just Drake. And he offered Avinash Dixit, my co-author, and I the standard 15% royalty. HAL VARIAN: 15%, yes. BARRY NALEBUFF: 15%. And I said, well, Drake, what about 30%? And patiently, he explained to me, well, there's production costs, editing costs, marketing costs. There's risk that we take. There's my salary. There's the overhead. If we gave you 30% royalty, we wouldn't make any money. I said, well, do you know what those numbers are? And it turns out he had a spreadsheet there. He had done the budget for this book. And those numbers added up to about $75,000. So I said, Drake, if we were to cover those costs-- instead of an advance, a retreat. If we were to pay you the $75,000, could we have the 30% royalty. He thinks about it. He says, yeah, actually. There goes my risk. That's in some sense our profit. And essentially, we're really partners in that case. So sure. Well, my co-author Professor Dixit-- he never sold more than 1,200 copies of any book he had written and wasn't so sure-- HAL VARIAN: Those are good books, too. I know them well. BARRY NALEBUFF: He wasn't so sure that this was going to be a good idea. And so he didn't-- he said, no, I'll just stick with the standard. And I followed suit. Of course, what I could have done is just put in $37.5 thousand and bought the extra half, if you like, from 15% to 22.5%. Or I could have put it in the whole $75,000 and got from 15% to 30%. I did neither. The book sold 500,000 copies. That mistake cost me over $1 million. However, I haven't made that same mistake on this book. And Michael Lewis, who you know from everything-- the fifth-- sorry, "Premonitions" is his new book to "Moneyball" to-- HAL VARIAN: Yeah. BARRY NALEBUFF: He has 17 books, all with WW Norton. HAL VARIAN: "New New Thing." BARRY NALEBUFF: The "New New Thing." And his new thing is to split things 50-50 with WW Norton. HAL VARIAN: Ah-ha. BARRY NALEBUFF: And so yes, actually, I think that's a better way of doing contracts with publishers. And it may sound a little bit crazy. But the truth is, what's the pie that's being created? I need the publisher to get the distribution, to get the editing, if you'd like. They need the content. Away we go. HAL VARIAN: Yes, it's amazing. There are so many deals in the book business on placement. For example, I remember placement of the book in airports. You may have gone through that negotiation, too. BARRY NALEBUFF: There's something I remember called "airports," where you used to go and get on planes and things. But I don't know. HAL VARIAN: [LAUGHS] Well, this is in the olden days. But in any event, the point is, basically, you have no bargaining power there-- at least in my experience, you don't. And it's all a question of getting volume and word of mouth out there. BARRY NALEBUFF: Actually, let's go back to Google a little bit on this. I'm not sure of that. Because remember, you don't just take the ad where they're offering you the highest price. You're taking the ad which you think people are going to click on and they're going to be happy about it. HAL VARIAN: Oh, yeah. BARRY NALEBUFF: And so the airport stores-- in some sense, I could pay for placement. But if there's no sales, that wasn't necessarily the right book for them to be putting on the shelf. HAL VARIAN: They would get sales, but the point is the bookstores in airports are typically part of a chain. And there's very little competition going on there. And there's kind of an immediate interest in buying. BARRY NALEBUFF: Remember, they're a monopolist. OK, I've got that. HAL VARIAN: Yes. BARRY NALEBUFF: But here's the thing. If two people are offering them $15,000 for placement and one of them is going to sell a lot more books-- HAL VARIAN: Yeah, yeah. Of course. I agree. BARRY NALEBUFF: They care about that just like Google cares not just about the price-- they also care about the click-through rate. HAL VARIAN: Well, but the point is, in this case, I care about the sales of the book because it's going to build the audience, build word of mouth, build all this other stuff. There are all of these spillover effects. And it's generally worth doing. Although you don't do it-- you often wait a little bit. At least in my books, they suggested waiting a little bit and not coming out with a zero-margin purchase right at the beginning. But I don't know if that's right or not. Again, it comes down to the numbers. BARRY NALEBUFF: My only point is there is some potential for negotiation. HAL VARIAN: Yeah, yeah. BARRY NALEBUFF: Because they don't care just about their price. They also care about the sell-through rate. HAL VARIAN: Yeah, yeah, yeah. All righty. Let's see. I think what we might do here-- I'm just looking in my list of questions. Honest Tea. BARRY NALEBUFF: We talked about that. HAL VARIAN: Yeah. So there's this issue of practical advice here. If you're negotiating a big deal-- or if I'm negotiating a big deal, should I hire a professional to do it for me? Now, obviously, you are the professional. So I'm not talking about that. But an ordinary person, not an economist, not an accountant, not a lawyer-- what's the best thing for him or her to do? BARRY NALEBUFF: "They." HAL VARIAN: Yes. BARRY NALEBUFF: So what I think they should do is work with a professional if it's feasible. Even in my case actually, I didn't want to negotiate the deal with Coca-Cola. It was terrible because it was way too high-stakes. I cared too much. And I want you to be objective here. And I could be much more objective when I'm negotiating for Hal then when I can for myself. The only reason why we didn't bring in investment bankers is Coke didn't want to turn this into an auction situation. And so they said, no investment bankers or we're not talking to you. HAL VARIAN: Ah. BARRY NALEBUFF: And OK. I had to take a choice. Am I willing to risk it or not? And so I was actually forced to do it myself, which-- otherwise, maybe I wouldn't have brought out the pie theory if I had had more professional advice. So I am a huge fan of putting an objective person in there as part of the negotiation. HAL VARIAN: So is it OK for me to say, but I want to be able to talk to my friend Barry Nalebuff before committing to a deal? BARRY NALEBUFF: Absolutely. HAL VARIAN: [LAUGHS] BARRY NALEBUFF: (CHUCKLING) Yeah. HAL VARIAN: The audience-- you've heard it there. So that's good. OK. But this distinction that you didn't want an investment banker, what-- BARRY NALEBUFF: No, I wanted it. They didn't want it. HAL VARIAN: That's right. That they didn't want an investment banker. So of these various professions we just ran through-- the investment banker, the lawyer, the accountant, the financial advisor, et cetera-- as a general statement, who would you go with? You'd go with the-- BARRY NALEBUFF: Oh, I would go with the lawyer. HAL VARIAN: With the lawyer? BARRY NALEBUFF: Yeah. And in particular, also, we had a lawyer who I think was a counselor in the true meaning of the word "counsel." And don't wait to get to know your lawyer when you're starting to do a deal. It's too late. HAL VARIAN: He's like that guy in the-- yeah. He's like that guy in "The Godfather," right? The Consigliere. BARRY NALEBUFF: Yeah. HAL VARIAN: Find a consigliere. BARRY NALEBUFF: So you want someone who understands you, who understands what your objectives are. And let me say that these negotiations got very tense. At one point, Nestlé had made us an offer. It got bounced by the CEO of Nestlé. They came back with a low offer. We said no. The person at Nestlé wrote to Seth saying that, Barry is destroying your family's future. And you shouldn't be letting him negotiate. This is malpractice-- so trying to split us up, in various ways. So these things can become very intense and very personal. Again, you want to have somebody often in between. On the other hand, if you can help people see things in terms of the pie, in some ways that pie can also be the intermediary for you all. HAL VARIAN: Yeah. BARRY NALEBUFF: And so effectively, it's like this impersonal mediator who's providing this impartial approach. HAL VARIAN: Let me switch to asking about one of your other books, which I think is unique in its category. And that is the "Message in a Bottle--" BARRY NALEBUFF: OK. HAL VARIAN: --which as I mentioned in my introduction-- [PHONE RINGING] --was a book-- just a minute. My phone is making sounds here. We got to stop that. BARRY NALEBUFF: That's what phones do. HAL VARIAN: Yeah. [RINGING STOPS] The case here-- as I explained it to the audience earlier, it was a comic book-- an illustrated novel, as we call them. BARRY NALEBUFF: Yep. HAL VARIAN: It was a great book. BARRY NALEBUFF: Graphic nonfiction. HAL VARIAN: Graphic nonfiction. OK. It was a great book-- really, really interesting. And I recommended it to all of the entrepreneurs that I work with because it shows you all the things that-- not all of them, but it shows you many things can go wrong. You can't count on things being persistent. You just have to roll with the punches-- at least that's the way I would interpret it. But what made you decide to write it as a comic book? BARRY NALEBUFF: Well, you said the word "unique." And I'd say there are a lot of books out there which are, how I built my business. And did the world need another one of those? Also, in some ways, let's have some fun writing it. Let's have some fun reading it. And one thing that's true about these graphic presentations is that every word counts. When you got a bubble and you can only put 19 words in there, you can't screw around with being verbose. And so the material just goes super quickly. It was remarkably useful for me to learn how to do this. Because after working with the graphic artist, I then worked with an animator. And the course created on Coursera uses lots of animation, which in some sense is the next step from just a graphic presentation. And so as a method for teaching, as a method for learning how to write, both of them were exceptionally useful. And I also think that the generation that we're selling this book to-- they grew up on graphic presentations. So one of the things is you meet your audience where they are, not where you are. HAL VARIAN: Sounds great. I think we're about ready to take a few questions from the audience here. BARRY NALEBUFF: Let's do it. HAL VARIAN: OK. Here we go. I have to read the question. "Is the "split the pie" approach applicable to all negotiation contexts? Or is it best suited for certain scenarios?" Great question. BARRY NALEBUFF: Yeah. It is easiest to apply in negotiations with two parties because there is where you can calculate the pie without too much difficulty. I think as you're starting to get more and more parties-- we do have a chapter which talks about multiparty negotiations, but I'll say it is more advanced and it's more complicated. So I would start out with thinking about it for two-party negotiations. And it isn't just issues of mergers, or buying domain names, or dividing pizzas. It's, any time you're having a negotiation start with what's the pie-- why are you doing this? What's the purpose of the two of you getting together? And the good news is that focus is on the positive. Instead of telling the other person why they're useless, you focus on why, together we're going to create something great. HAL VARIAN: What about negotiations where dollars are not involved? I want to go out to this restaurant. You want to go out to that restaurant. We both want to eat together. It's like the battle of the sexes in game theory. So does that impact anything in terms of the pie negotiation? BARRY NALEBUFF: So one of the lessons that we say in the book is to give the other side what they want. And I say that not because I'm generous, not because I'm nice, but because if they get what they want then I can get what I want. So what does that mean? Figure out who wants the restaurant more than the other. And let that person get it and then compensate you in some other way, whether it means they're doing the dishes, taking the dog out for the last walk, late at night-- whatever it is. We're not here necessarily negotiating about money. So think about it this way. If Hal and I are splitting three servings of beets and three servings of broccoli, it doesn't make any sense for each of us to get one and a half scoops of each because I don't like beets. HAL VARIAN: [CHUCKLES] BARRY NALEBUFF: And I'm assuming Hal does. And so Hal you get all the beets, and I should get all the broccoli. HAL VARIAN: All right. So it gives you an extra dimension to the negotiation that you didn't have with the straight money. BARRY NALEBUFF: So create this other dimension. And if somebody cares more about some decision, don't fight over it. Give it to them. And the corollary, of course, is if somebody really doesn't want to give something up, don't make them. Because effectively, then you're taking away from them something they really want, which means they're not going to give you what it is you want. HAL VARIAN: Yeah. BARRY NALEBUFF: It also means you have to answer as well as ask questions. So people think you have to answer questions because of reciprocity-- the other side will stop answering your questions if you don't answer theirs. There's another reason to answer questions, which is you want the other side to give you what it is you want. And they won't know that unless you help them by answering questions. HAL VARIAN: So what about the threat point? Let's go back to the Coke negotiation. The threat point is, you don't reach a deal, but then you're going to trot over to Pepsi, right, or some other soft drink beverage. BARRY NALEBUFF: Yeah. HAL VARIAN: So it's not just that you get zero out of it. You learned a lot in this negotiation. And you can apply that knowledge in dealing with competitors. BARRY NALEBUFF: Absolutely. And here's another case where you have to be really careful about how you go about this. So one other company that we negotiated with, a teabag company, basically gave us an offer that we weren't particularly keen about and then said, well, if you don't take this offer, we're going to crush you like these tea leaves in my hand. And one, we weren't really convinced that was true because just because you're good in tea bags doesn't mean you're good in bottled tea. But also, do we really want to sell our baby to such a jerk? HAL VARIAN: [CHUCKLES] BARRY NALEBUFF: That's not the kind of person who we want to be working with in the future, who we want to entrust our company to. HAL VARIAN: Right. This is the first decision among many if we get together. BARRY NALEBUFF: Yeah. In fact, it's all-- and by the way, this is a lesson for you who are negotiating salaries, negotiating with your boss. Basically, they often really learn about you for the first time through the negotiation. So don't be a jerk. Now, what did Coca-Cola say in comparison? They said, we looked at 500 companies. We did a deep dive into 30. We've met with five. You are our number one choice. You're the company we want to buy. However, it's important for you to realize that we have been given a mandate from the board to buy a tea company. This happened right after the Coke and Nestlé-- the Nestea partnership broke up. So for the first time in 25 years, Coke was able to buy a tea company on their own. And so therefore, you should understand that, whatever happens, we are going to get a tea company. We want it to be yours. Now, implicit in that is a threat, right, which is, if you don't sell to us, we'll buy these other people and compete with you. But they're not saying it that way. They're saying it in the nicest possible way. And so it's important to help the other side appreciate their BATNA, but you don't want to do it in a way that comes across as a threat. HAL VARIAN: Yep. Let's take another question. Ignacio-- "does your friend care about the cost to society of feeding the troll?" BARRY NALEBUFF: So remember, my friend was me. Yes, I do. I feel bad about that. But it's one of the reasons also why I sure as heck wasn't going to go and let him get more than half the pie. So the idea of letting the troll get more than half of the $1,300-- absolutely not. No. And look, if we go back in time to the Cuban Missile Crisis, do I really want to negotiate with the Russians? Well, it's saving the world. And yeah, OK, we got rid of the nuclear missiles in Turkey. And that's better than having nuclear war. Do I want to negotiate with Putin over Ukraine's membership in NATO? No, but do I want war there? No. And one of the things we appreciate is that some people can destroy pie. And preventing them from destroying pie is actually a way of creating pie. So at some point, you have to think about your reputation effects. Because of course, I want to have a reputation of not negotiating with dictators, with terrorists because that opens up people in the future. HAL VARIAN: But it has to be done. You can't walk away from that negotiation. There's got to be the attempt made. BARRY NALEBUFF: Absolutely. The question is, can you keep it private? Is that a possibility or not? HAL VARIAN: Yeah. How about another question out there? OK. "What should be your friend's strategy if the friend did not have heard of ICANN and your friend is short on time?" OK. So this is a person who wants a domain name. They don't know what ICANN is, but they really need to get it by the end of the week. BARRY NALEBUFF: So just again, that friend-- remember-- is me. HAL VARIAN: That's you. That's you. BARRY NALEBUFF: [CHUCKLES] Just we haven't really got that idea across somehow or these are-- HAL VARIAN: Well, they may have entered these questions before [INAUDIBLE]. BARRY NALEBUFF: Early on. So a couple of things. One is, what's the alternative name-- so instead of makeroates.com, maker-oates.com. HAL VARIAN: Yeah. BARRY NALEBUFF: Realizing that, actually, most people don't even type in URLs anyway. They're going to Google the name "Maker Oates." And if "maker-oates" is the one where all the traffic is going, that's what's going to show up in terms of the Google site. And no, in terms of being short on time, the truth is that the other side has no idea whether or not I'm in a hurry, I'm not in a hurry. One thing that's advantageous is that if you Google the name of the business there's no evidence that it's actually running. So the person doesn't know, am I just thinking about this now, what is going to be the future of this company. So I think the other person is every bit as concerned about time that I am. Because basically, the person is going to figure, if I don't do this deal with him, I'm going to come up with some other name for the company, some other hyphen thing-- some makeroates.us.biz-- and it'll be good enough. So that would be my strategy in this particular case. HAL VARIAN: So I have read or I've heard that in the Nixon and Kissinger deals with the Chinese way back whenever that was-- 20 years ago or 30 years ago-- Nixon instructed Kissinger to tell the Chinese he was crazy. Nixon wasn't rational. He didn't do any of these calculations. He didn't know anything about pies. Look, you don't know what crazy thing he's going to do. So what is that strategy-- how does that strategy of signaling to the other party that you could be crazy? BARRY NALEBUFF: There's a great story about this more recently. I'm blanking on his name. But the Greek minister of finance-- HAL VARIAN: Oh, yes. BARRY NALEBUFF: --during the whole currency crisis talked about the rational advantage of acting irrational to get the other people to give in to your demands. The problem is that you've got to be a real idiot if you talk about it doing that way. HAL VARIAN: [CHUCKLES] BARRY NALEBUFF: Because it's like, OK, I just read that piece where it says you rationally are planning to act irrationally. So much for that, Mr. Hyper-rational. And part of the problem is, since rational people do have an incentive to pretend to be irrational, I'm not sure I'm going to be buying it when I see that happen. Moreover I'm also going to say to the other party, help me understand your reasoning here. And just saying, I want the $900 because I want the $900, isn't a great reason. HAL VARIAN: Yep. So it might be a reasonable strategy for politicians but not for economists, I guess. BARRY NALEBUFF: Yeah. Or if two people are playing that game, that's an easy way to get no deal. So again, you want to put fire out with water. But also, it's not-- it seems appropriate to say to somebody, look, you may be irrational, but you know what? This is my position. And so tell me where I'm wrong. And if you can explain to me where I'm wrong, I'm prepared to change. But you're just saying things that are arbitrary. Now, if I know that's who I'm negotiating with from the start, OK, I can play that game too. But it's unlikely to be very productive. HAL VARIAN: OK. We got a couple more questions coming in here. Next question. OK. "Are there particular situations you believe BATNA should not be revealed? Is there a framework on how to disclose information and when?" [INAUDIBLE] a former student by the way. This is a former student. BARRY NALEBUFF: Yeah, so thank you, Google, for hiring Logan. Thank you, Logan, for-- HAL VARIAN: OK. [LAUGHS] BARRY NALEBUFF: --coming in here. I think in general, people don't talk enough about what their real interests are. So in one example of a case that I taught with Logan, a person is selling a gas station. And their reason was to take a trip around the world. Should they reveal that or not? Well, the buyer knows that they're selling it for some reason. There's good reasons, and there are bad reasons. A bad reason is there's a leak in the underground storage tank, and it's going to become a superfund site. A good reason is, hey, I want to travel around the world. That's not bad news. And people keep things that are hidden that should be revealed. Because once I understand what your objective is, I want to put you on that boat. Because if you go in the boat, I get to buy the station. And then I learn that you don't have a job when you come back. And I think you're a great manager. So what I want to do is give you a job when you return. That means you really want to sell the station to me. Now, does that mean that I need to tell you of a boat payment coming due in, oh, 35 minutes, and if it doesn't happen, I'm going to lose everything? Well, by the way, if I really need the money in 35 minutes, yeah, actually. I probably should. HAL VARIAN: Yeah. BARRY NALEBUFF: If we've agreed to split the pie, then I think we're in a much safer position in terms of revealing our BATNA. If, in fact, I think the other person is going to try and push me to my BATNA because they're the jerk, the irrational type, the zero-sum mindset type, then I think I have to keep those things hidden. So can we get the framework established up front? And can we also be behaving in a way which has some reciprocity? And you can also reveal things in a st-- like, my BATNA begins with a 4, as opposed to, it's $436,912. HAL VARIAN: Yeah, so you can partially reveal it. Yeah. Next question. What do we got here? From Sofia-- oh, it's not a question. It's an exclamation point. "Thanks for coming today, Barry. What advice do you have for those who struggle to make negotiations?" BARRY NALEBUFF: Yeah. One is to practice. And to practice one pl-- look. OK. What's the clear advice? We don't have to kid around here. HAL VARIAN: [LAUGHS] Buy the book. BARRY NALEBUFF: Buy the book. Right? What can I say? So I'm guessing that Sofia is the kind of person who doesn't want to be taken advantage of but doesn't want to act like a jerk. And so yeah, you're uncomfortable because people are going to make you uncomfortable in negotiations. And that's why you need to have this alternative. So there are case studies in the book. The Coursera course also gives you chances to practice with other people taking the class and see what happens. And then you can watch debriefs of how your negotiation went compared to other people's. And so it's a little bit like those alternative paths of the universe in terms of their forking. And you can see if you had made a threat, if you had made an ultimatum how that could have been diffused, what happens if you lie, and so on. HAL VARIAN: Yeah. My friend who was a lawyer who taught negotiations in law school was very keen on running these same class experiments. I think they're a great idea. Because partly, people can get over the fear, or the anxiety, or whatever emotional feeling they have and treat it as a rational negotiation. BARRY NALEBUFF: They could also discover that acting like a jerk doesn't help them. HAL VARIAN: Yeah. BARRY NALEBUFF: One, because they're actually generally not very good at being a jerk. And two, they can just see how things blow up. And so then they can get more comfortable with becoming their true self in a negotiation. HAL VARIAN: OK. Now I have a message here. More questions came in, but that may be delayed from a few minutes ago. So I think we said we'd go until 1:30. Is that right? Everybody-- BARRY NALEBUFF: I think [INAUDIBLE].. HAL VARIAN: We should negotiate that. Yeah. Two more minutes. All right. A message came in. Two more minutes. So it's your last two minutes. Do you want to sum things up? When will we be able to buy your book-- all these things. BARRY NALEBUFF: Yesterday was the book's birthday. HAL VARIAN: Ah. BARRY NALEBUFF: So it came out. And you can go to splitthepiebook.com. I haven't negotiated with the troll who owns splitthepie.com yet, but that's something to happen in the future. And there, you can see some videos, a little excerpt of Chapter 1. My, I guess, big takeaways are don't just ask-- ask with a reason. The way to figure out the reason is to start with what is the pie-- to understand what's being created in terms of the negotiation. If you can agree with people to split the pie, then you can turn your attention on making the pie bigger. And you made the pie bigger already because you're going to have a deal. So that's worth a lot just to begin with. But you can make it a better deal. Having said that, understand that this is not the way the world negotiates. I'm not describing a common practice here. We're trying to change the world. So in order to do that, you're going to have to be able to convince others. That starts with convincing yourself. So this is a good way to start doing that. And unlike most of the other books on negotiation, this is a book that works well when the other side has read it too. And so it's not like, oh, I've got some little secret here about, I'm going to anchor high. Well, I'm going to anchor high. Oh, and now it's actually worse for both of us. So when both people understand what they're really negotiating about, the whole negotiation should go much smoother. HAL VARIAN: Raise the anchor but not too far. BARRY NALEBUFF: There we go. HAL VARIAN: All right. Thank you so much, Barry. It's been great hearing you, great seeing you. Best of luck with the book. I'm going to run right out and get one. BARRY NALEBUFF: Just one? Just one? HAL VARIAN: [LAUGHS] For starters. BARRY NALEBUFF: There we go. Hal, it's such a pleasure to be back with you again. HAL VARIAN: Yeah. BARRY NALEBUFF: And let's not wait another however long it is. To be continued. Let's make some big pies together and split them. Thanks to everybody for joining us. HAL VARIAN: All right. Sounds good. Sounds great. Thank you. [MUSIC PLAYING]
